title: "He abused me" (3–6)
hook: hatred never ceases by hatred, only by not-hatred; this is an old rule (Dhammapada 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, verses one and two: the mind comes first, and your line was the wheel follows the ox. Did you catch a thought steering your mood? Day one hundred fifty-nine.
screen: `THE MIND COMES FIRST — THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.`

segments.voice: It's two in the morning and you're awake, replaying it. What they said at the meeting. The look on their face. What you should have said back. You've replayed it so many times it's worn smooth, like a stone in a pocket, and every time you turn it over, it still stings. Almost everybody carries one of these. Some people carry them for decades. The Dhammapada's third verse describes exactly this, word for word, as if it had been listening at the bedroom door. Today: “he abused me.”
screen: `2AM. REPLAYING IT.` → `A STONE WORN SMOOTH.` → `IT STILL STINGS.`

segments.voice: Verse three, in Müller's English: “‘He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,’—in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.” Verse four is its twin: in those who don't harbor such thoughts, hatred will cease. Notice where the problem is placed. Not only in what the other person did, but in the replay. The verse doesn't say the insult didn't happen. It says hatred lives on in the harboring. Then verse five, one of the most quoted lines in all of Buddhism: “hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love.” Müller wrote love. The Pali word is averena, which means by non-hatred, by not hating back. It's quieter than love, and maybe more realistic: you don't have to feel warm toward the person, you just stop feeding the fire. The verse ends: this is an old rule. In the Pali, an eternal law. Not a Buddhist invention, but how hatred has always worked. The commentary sets verse five in a story of two women whose rivalry ran on through lifetime after lifetime, each taking revenge for the last, until the Buddha stopped the cycle. And verse six belongs to a famous quarrel among the monks of Kosambi, who split over a small matter of rules. Verse six says, roughly, that people forget we all come to an end here, and those who remember it let their quarrels settle. So chapter one gives two tools for the 2am replay: notice that the hatred lives in the harboring, and remember how short all of this is.
screen: `VERSE THREE: THE REPLAY.` · `HATRED LIVES IN THE HARBORING.` · `VERSE FIVE: BY NOT HATING BACK.` · `REMEMBER HOW SHORT THIS IS.` · then, large: `HATRED ENDS BY NOT-HATRED.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Now, gently, let a small old grudge come to mind. Not the biggest one. A mild one. Notice the sentence that comes with it, your own version of “he abused me, he robbed me.” Hear it once. Then, instead of replaying it, feel what it does in the body: the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach. Breathe into that place. You don't have to forgive anyone right now. Just try not feeding it for the length of this sit. When the replay starts again, come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
“He abused me.” The thought that keeps hatred alive, in verses three to six, and the old rule that only not-hatred ends it.
Your line: hatred ends by not-hatred. Today, when the old grudge thought starts its replay, drop it once. Just once. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 159 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WIND AND THE ROCK.`

howItsDone: Verse five of the Dhammapada is one of the most often recited Buddhist verses; teachers use verses three to six to show that resentment is kept alive by rehearsing it, and ended by not answering hatred with hatred.

match.prompt: match the pieces of verses three to six.
pairs: the replay: he abused me, he robbed me
by non-hatred, by not hating back

myth: the Pali of verse five says hatred ceases by love
Müller wrote love; the Pali averena means by non-hatred, by not hating back.
verse five calls this an old rule, or an eternal law
the Pali calls it sanantano: how hatred has always worked.
verse three says the insult never really happened
it says hatred lives on in those who harbor the thought.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. the monks of Kosambi are quarreling and, when you try to make peace, they tell you to stay out of it. what do you do?
options: leave them and go off alone to the forest.
take one side and settle it.
fork.reveal: in the Vinaya's telling, he left and spent time alone in the forest. the lay people then stopped supporting the quarreling monks until they made peace.

original.note: Pali: by non-hatred, from verse five: hatred is calmed by non-hatred.

trapdoor: what you thought: verse five means you have to love the person who hurt you.
what it means: hatred stops when you stop feeding it and don't hate back.
what a scholar hears: 'na hi verena verani sammantidha kudacanam, averena ca sammanti, esa dhammo sanantano': averena is non-enmity, and sanantano is ancient or eternal.

sources.quoted: 'He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,'--in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.
hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga X, the Kosambi quarrel; Dhammapada-atthakatha, stories for verses 5 and 6

notes: Check verses 3 and 5 word for word against Müller's SBE 10 text (the dash before 'in those' is rendered here as an em dash).
Verse 5 story (Kali the yakkhini and the barren wife) is summarized in one sentence only; verse 6 attached to the Kosambi quarrel. Confirm.
Fork: the Buddha withdrawing to the Parileyyaka forest and lay supporters withholding alms until the Kosambi monks reconciled (Mahavagga X). Confirm.
Practice invites noticing a mild grudge, explicitly not requiring forgiveness.
